title: Not Invented Here
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note takes aim at "not invented here" syndrome — the reflexive rejection of good ideas simply because they originated outside a team's own walls. It argues that the market leaders across industry history are rarely originators; they are organizations that borrowed ideas from elsewhere and executed them with more polish than anyone else. The piece traces the syndrome's root to team leaders who treat outside learning as a sign of weakness, and shows how that posture, though often disguised as team pride, is really a form of arrogance that undermines the team's own success. Using the memorable "toothbrush theory" analogy, the author distinguishes between practices people won't share (toothbrushes) and the far larger category of practices that can and should be freely borrowed (toothpaste). The essay ends with a call to replace "not invented here" with a "proudly found elsewhere" mentality.
points: Market-leading organizations are rarely originators — they succeed by borrowing ideas from outside and executing them with more polish than the source.
"Not invented here" syndrome is strongest in teams with rich history and tight culture, precisely where team pride masks a costly form of arrogance.
The "toothbrush theory" distinguishes ideas people won't share (toothbrushes) from the much larger category of practices that should be freely copied (toothpaste).
Leaders set the tone: team leaders who treat outside ideas as a threat infect the whole team with the same false pride.
quotes: In the history of organizational success, the enterprises that dominate tend to flawlessly execute on ideas that were created elsewhere.

The xenophobia of ideas "not invented here" cripples organizations over the long run, and often allows competitors to destroy longstanding value by embracing better ideas and executing them with polish.
The reality is that the leader's unwillingness to acknowledge or value the work of others outside the team is a form of arrogance that weakens the very thing it is meant to protect.
Everyone wants one. Everyone needs one. But no one wants to use someone else's.
Thankfully, most team success solutions and practices are more like toothpaste than toothbrushes.
It's time for the monopoly of "not invented here" to end in your organization. Not everything is a toothbrush.
